claims.text: Optimizing microstructure through controlled processing can improve the ductility of metals and alloys.
Rolling and annealing enhance grain-boundary mobility.
Rolling and annealing reduce dislocation density.
The proposed material is a polycrystalline copper alloy with mixed grain sizes and orientations.
The proposed experiment uses in-situ TEM during tensile testing at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 and 20°C.
The tensile test is limited to a maximum strain of 20%.
Enhanced grain-boundary mobility permits more efficient stress redistribution.
Reduced dislocation density increases strain hardening.
Enhanced grain-boundary mobility, reduced dislocation density, increased strain hardening, and delayed necking improve ductility.
The optimized copper alloy will exhibit at least a 25% relative increase in elongation at break.
The comparator is a conventional polycrystalline copper alloy with a random microstructure.
A measured ductility improvement below 10% would falsify the hypothesis.
The magnitude of ductility improvement depends on composition, processing history, and testing conditions.
Precipitates and texture may also influence the ductility response.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies rolling and annealing as the microstructure-optimizing intervention, but the stated intervention is in-situ TEM tensile testing, which observes deformation rather than implementing the claimed rolling or annealing treatment.
